unit.unitTitle: The Digital World and Future Innovation
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9: The Digital World and Future Innovation! In this unit you will explore how digital technology, robotics, and innovative farming are reshaping daily life across East Africa and the wider world. You will read about young people who use smartphones, coding skills, and creative thinking to solve real problems in their communities. Through reading, writing, speaking, and grammar activities, you will sharpen your English skills while thinking critically about the role of technology in our lives.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary companion and learn the thirty unit words a few at a time, saying each example aloud. Work through the six grammar lessons, from the present perfect with just and reported speech to conditionals, complex noun phrases and the verb patterns that follow adjectives and prepositions. Read "Smart Farms and Digital Dreams", the radio interview and the two-part story "Shadows in the Feed", answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the writing workshop (debate essay, digital detox diary or future farming report), the speaking tasks and the activities, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: Smart Farms and Digital Dreams
readings.theme: The Digital World and Future Innovation
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In recent years, digital technology has begun to reveal new possibilities for communities across East Africa. From busy capital cities to small farming towns, young innovators are finding versatile ways to use smartphones, sensors, and coding to solve problems that once seemed impossible. One of the most exciting areas of change is future farming — using technology to grow more food with fewer resources.
In one small farming town, a group of secondary-school students conceived a plan to help local farmers. They had noticed that many families were struggling because rainfall had become unpredictable. Crops failed, and food prices grew worse every season. The students decided to acquire basic coding skills and build a simple weather-monitoring app. Their teacher, Mr. Rohan, introduced them to rudimentary electronics — small sensors that could measure temperature, humidity, and soil moisture.
At first, some adults were sceptical. A local shopkeeper said that students were too young to build anything useful. He told them that technology would not replace hard work. But the students were not agitated by the criticism. They determined that if they worked together, they could prove the doubters wrong. Unless they tried, they would never know what was possible.
Within three months, the team had built a working prototype. The app collected data from small sensors placed in the soil and sent alerts to farmers' phones. If the soil was too dry, the app told the farmer to water the crops. Unless the temperature dropped below a safe level, the system stayed quiet. One farmer, Amara, reported that she had just saved an entire field of maize thanks to an early warning from the app.
Word about the project spread quickly. People from neighbouring villages converged on the school to see demonstrations. A journalist from a regional radio station interviewed the students. She asked them how they had learned to code. Imani, the team leader, replied that they had taught themselves using free online tutorials. She said that anyone with a phone and internet access could learn the same skills.
The project also introduced a drone that could photograph fields from above. By comparing images taken at different times, the students could spot which parts of a field were healthy and which were struggling. This kind of analysis, once obscure and expensive, was now adequate for a school team with basic equipment.
Mr. Rohan told a visiting teacher that the students had just completed their most ambitious test. He reported that if the government supported similar programmes, thousands of farms could benefit. He said that unless young people were given opportunities to innovate, the country would fall behind.
Today, the students' app is used by over two hundred farmers in three districts. The team has not stopped innovating. They are now working on a solar-powered irrigation system — a complex, automated, solar-powered water-delivery device — that could change farming in the region for ever. As Imani says, "Technology is not magic. It is just people solving problems, step by step."

readings.title: A Radio Interview: The School Coding Club
readings.theme: The Digital World and Future Innovation
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Interviewer: Welcome to the programme. Tell us about the coding club at your school.
Kofi: We started the club last term with just eight students. Now everyone wants to join. We have just learned how to build simple apps using free software.
Interviewer: What have you built so far?
Kofi: Our first project was a rudimentary quiz app for younger students. It asks questions about maths and science, and it gives hints if you get stuck. We also built a small weather station using a versatile sensor kit our teacher ordered online.
Interviewer: Has anyone been sceptical about the club?
Kofi: At first, some parents said that coding was a waste of time. They told us that we should focus on traditional subjects. But when they saw what we had conceived and built, they changed their minds. My father said that he was proud of what we had acquired.
Interviewer: What advice would you give to students who want to start a similar club?
Kofi: Start with what you have. Unless you try, you will never know what you can build. If you have a phone and internet access, you already have adequate resources to begin.
Interviewer: That is a blunt but honest answer. Thank you, Kofi, and good luck to the club.
Kofi: Thank you for having me.

readings.title: Shadows in the Feed, part 1
readings.theme: The Digital World and Future Innovation
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The compound walls were cream-coloured, edged with climbing vines. From the rooftop of Amal's block of flats, the city skyline looked sharp and full of life — construction cranes beside old water towers, taxis jostling through roundabouts, teenagers laughing as they left tutoring centres.
Amal sat astride the bench's armrest, sketchpad on her lap. She had just finished a rough drawing of the sunset when her younger brother barged in.
"Did you hear about the boy from the north end?" Idris asked.
"No," Amal replied, barely looking up.
"He was ostracised from school. They say he was caught hacking the computer lab!"
Amal blinked. "Hacking? Like, code or stealing?"
"Both, maybe. No one knows. It's all over every feed in the city."
She sighed. The whole neighbourhood buzzed with digital gossip. But Amal preferred fact over fiction.
At school the next morning, news spread faster than light. Amal overheard classmates comparing the boy's story.
"I heard he's a fugitive, hiding somewhere near the bus depot."
"No, no," said another. "He's in custody. His uncle revealed it in a live video."
"People just want to bamboozle each other with drama," Amal muttered.
During lunch, she sat with her best friend, Nora, who was versatile in everything from coding to poetry.
"We don't even know him," Nora said. "Why is everyone so quick to judge?"
"I want to know what really happened," Amal said. "Not what the feeds say."
Later, she spoke with her tech club mentor, Mr. Tariq, a patient, blunt man who ran a small robotics lab on the school's second floor.
"You want the real story?" he said. "Then do what smart people do — acquire real information."
"How?"
"Start asking. But gently. With care."
Amal began by reaching out to Sana, a quiet girl who had been close to the accused student.
"His name's Zane," Sana said. "He's in the year above us. He's... different. Eccentric, maybe. Always coding, building circuits from old radios. But not dangerous."
"Then why was he blamed?"
"There was a lapse in the exam server last week. People panicked. Teachers needed someone to blame."
Amal listened, her mind forming connections.
"What was his demeanour like that day?" she asked.
"Calm. Maybe too calm."
Zane's silence had become a blank canvas for gossip. Some said he had confessed. Others claimed he had vanished.
That evening, Amal couldn't stop thinking. Her mind was conceiving a plan: an article for the school blog.
She spent the night comparing rumours, tracing message threads, and speaking with classmates who had known Zane.
She even visited the dusty IT server room the next morning, asking for archived network logs. The technician, surprised but curious, let her observe. There, among the logs, was a timestamp proving Zane had emailed a teacher minutes before the system crash. The message described a wireless experiment — not a hack.
By Friday, she had just completed a rough draft: "Misjudged in the Digital Age."
In it, she presented evidence that Zane had been working on a separate wireless project — one that accidentally overloaded the lab's router. He wasn't a hacker. Just a curious student caught in a tech lapse.
She explained how bias grows in silence. She used phrases like "a lull in truth" and "an obscure, misunderstood project." Her language was careful — not to excuse, but to question.

readings.title: Shadows in the Feed, part 2
readings.theme: The Digital World and Future Innovation
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The blog post was uploaded on Saturday morning. It caused instant discussion.
In the school library on Monday, students were converging at the computers.
"Have you read it?"
"Yeah. I didn't know Zane had actually shared his plans with the computer teacher before!"
"Neither did I. The post says the logs prove it."
Zane hadn't been a hacker. He had been misunderstood. Even the head of IT commented, saying the article helped ease tension.
By Monday afternoon, Zane's name was cleared. He was exonerated by school officials and invited back.
Still, the damage had changed him. Amal saw him during robotics club — quieter, more cautious.
"You're back," she said.
He nodded. "It's weird. Like walking through fog."
"I'm glad you're here. I almost didn't write that article," Amal confessed.
"It helped," Zane replied. "Not just me. People are listening more carefully now."
Later, Mr. Tariq congratulated Amal. "It's not easy to speak against the crowd. It takes guts."
"It was difficult to determine what to omit," Amal said. "Too much, and I'd agitate people. Too little, and I'd hide the point."
He nodded. "But you chose well. That's journalism."
Weeks later, Amal was selected to present at the regional Young Writers' Forum. She prepared a multimedia talk titled "Perception vs. Reality: A Student's Dilemma."
During her presentation, she used a rudimentary animation to show how rumours spread. She included screenshots, student quotes, and even a short comparison between how Zane had been treated and how another student, who had admitted to copying an essay months earlier, had been quietly forgiven.
After her talk, a boy from another school approached her.
"I've just started a youth podcast. Would you consider guesting?"
Amal smiled. "Let me check with my parents."
"Of course."
In the following weeks, her episode aired. She spoke about the need to recognise misinformation and to give people space to explain.
One listener messaged: "Your story helped me reconnect with a cousin I'd ostracised. I realised I never asked him for his side."
Another wrote, "My sister was wrongly blamed at school last year. After hearing you, I realised how deeply that affected her."
For Amal, it wasn't fame she wanted. It was clarity.
And in the city she called home, where internet cables crossed old alleyways and stories raced through smart devices, clarity was sometimes the rarest thing of all.
A month later, Amal found herself sitting on that same rooftop bench, sketchpad in hand. The evening air carried the sounds of traffic and distant radios, and Idris was back from school, this time holding a drone kit their uncle had posted from another town.
"Can you help me build this?" he asked.
She looked at the box, then at her sketchbook, and smiled.
"Let's build it — and write about it afterwards. But first, we do it right. Step by step. No shortcuts."
In that moment, Amal understood something simple but powerful: clarity doesn't always come in a rush. Sometimes it comes slowly, piece by piece — just like a story, or a life.

grammar.title: Present Perfect with Just, and Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: The present perfect with just shows that an action happened only moments ago, while reported speech lets us relay what someone said by shifting the tense back one step — two patterns the digital world uses constantly for fresh updates and second-hand news.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Part 1 — Present perfect + just: use has (he, she, it) or have (I, you, we, they) + just + past participle: "She has just uploaded the code."; "They have just finished the app." Just sits before the past participle, and it never pairs with a finished-time phrase such as yesterday.
Part 2 — Reported speech: to report what someone said, remove the quotation marks, change the pronouns and move the tense back one step: "I have built an app." becomes She said that she had built an app; "The students will succeed." becomes Mr. Rohan said that the students would succeed. To report a question, use statement word order with asked how or asked whether: "How did you learn to code?" becomes She asked how they had learned to code. Reported questions end without a question mark.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving the tense unshifted ("She said that she has built an app") or keeping question word order in a reported question ("He asked did they use sensors" instead of "He asked whether they used sensors").
grammar.memoryTip: Just means moments ago — fresh as a notification that has just appeared on your screen. When you report speech later, step every tense back one, like moving a bookmark one page back.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete with the present perfect + just: 1) They ______ (just / finish) building the prototype. 2) I ______ (just / download) the new coding software. 3) He ______ (just / arrive) at the robotics workshop. 4) We ______ (just / receive) the sensor data from the farm. 5) She ______ (just / complete) her digital detox diary.
Part B — change into reported speech: 6) Amara said, "The app has just saved my crops." 7) The journalist asked, "How did you build the prototype?" 8) Mr. Rohan said, "We will test the drone next week." 9) A farmer asked, "Can the app work without internet?" 10) Imani said, "I am learning to code every day."
Part C — report each sentence: 11) The teacher said, "The students have just finished the coding project." 12) Imani told the journalist, "I will present our app at the science fair." 13) A parent asked, "Is the app safe for children to use?" 14) The engineer said, "We can build a better drone next year." 15) Daniel asked his classmate, "Where did you learn to programme?" 16) Amara said, "I am using the app every day on my farm."

===
Self-Check Answer Key
Part A (present perfect + just): 1) have just finished 2) have just downloaded 3) has just arrived 4) have just received 5) has just completed
Part B (reported speech): 6) Amara said that the app had just saved her crops. 7) The journalist asked how they had built the prototype. 8) Mr. Rohan said that they would test the drone the following week (tense steps back one; pronoun and time reference adjust to the new speaker/time). 9) A farmer asked whether the app could work without internet. 10) Imani said that she was learning to code every day.
Part C (report each sentence): 11) The teacher said that the students had just finished the coding project. 12) Imani told the journalist that she would present their app at the science fair. 13) A parent asked whether the app was safe for children to use. 14) The engineer said that they could build a better drone the following year. 15) Daniel asked his classmate where they had learned to programme. 16) Amara said that she was using the app every day on her farm.
Self-check method: for every answer, confirm (a) the verb tense has moved back one step from the original quote, and (b) pronouns/possessives have shifted to match who is now speaking, exactly as shown in the models above.

grammar.title: Connectives, and Conditionals with If and Unless
grammar.explanation: Connectives such as because, so that, although and therefore link ideas into clear, logical arguments, while conditional sentences with if and unless describe a possible situation and its likely result.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Part 1 — Connectives: because gives a reason ("The farmers use the app because it sends weather alerts."); so that shows purpose ("She coded the programme so that it would run on low-cost phones."); although shows contrast ("Although the internet was slow, the students submitted their project."); therefore shows a result ("The sensor detected dry soil; therefore, the app sent a watering alert.").
Part 2 — First conditional: if + present simple, then will + base verb: "If we use technology wisely, it will help our community."; "If the soil is too dry, the app will send an alert." Unless means if not: "Unless the temperature drops, the crops will survive."; "You will not learn to code unless you practise every day."
grammar.commonMistake: Putting will inside the if-clause ("If we will use technology wisely, it will help us") or doubling the negative after unless ("Unless we don't reduce screen time") — unless already means if not.
grammar.memoryTip: Connectives connect — they are the glue between ideas — and unless carries a built-in not: swap it for "if... not" to test whether your sentence still makes sense.
grammar.practice:
Part A — fill in because, so that, although or therefore: 1) I backed up my files ______ I would not lose them. 2) ______ the battery was low, the drone still completed its scan. 3) She shared her code online ______ other students could learn from it. 4) The app crashed ______ there was a bug in the latest update. 5) The internet was slow; ______, the download took much longer than expected.
Part B — complete each conditional: 6) If farmers ______ (use) the app, they will save water. 7) Unless the students ______ (work) together, the project will fail. 8) The drone will take off if the battery ______ (be) fully charged. 9) Unless you ______ (check) your sources, you might share misinformation. 10) If she ______ (learn) to code, she will build her own app.
Part C — choose the correct form: 11) If we ______ (not limit) our screen time, our health will suffer. 12) Unless the internet connection ______ (improve), online learning will be difficult. 13) Farmers will lose their crops if the warning system ______ (fail). 14) Unless schools ______ (teach) coding, students will miss important skills. 15) If artificial intelligence ______ (continue) to develop, many jobs will change. 16) You will not spot misinformation unless you ______ (check) multiple sources.

===
Self-Check Answer Key
Part A (connectives): 1) so that 2) Although 3) so that 4) because 5) therefore
Part B (conditionals — present simple in the if/unless clause): 6) use 7) work 8) is 9) check 10) learns
Part C (choose the correct form): 11) do not limit 12) improves 13) fails 14) teach 15) continues 16) check
Self-check method: for Part A, ask whether the blank gives a reason (because), a purpose (so that), a contrast (although) or a result (therefore). For Parts B and C, confirm the if/unless clause uses present simple (never "will"), matching subject-verb agreement (singular subject takes -s: improves, fails, continues, learns; plural subject takes base form: use, work, check, teach, do not limit).

grammar.title: Either / Neither / Both
grammar.explanation: Either, neither and both let you compare two options precisely: either chooses one of two, neither rejects both, and both takes the two together.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Either means one of two options and takes a singular noun and verb: "You can use either the laptop or the tablet."; "Either device is suitable." Neither means not one and not the other and also takes a singular verb: "Neither app is working properly."; "Neither option is available." Both means the two together and takes a plural noun and verb: "Both apps have been updated."; "Both systems are connected."
grammar.commonMistake: Giving neither a plural verb ("Neither options are good") or pairing both with a singular noun ("Both app are updated") — neither stays singular, both stays plural.
grammar.memoryTip: Either sounds like election — choose one; neither means not one of the two; both is the pair together, so it always takes a plural verb.
grammar.practice:
Fill in with either, neither or both: 1) You can connect to ______ the Wi-Fi or the mobile data. (one of two) 2) ______ of the chargers is working, so we need a new one. (not one, not the other) 3) ______ students passed the coding test — well done! (the two together) 4) I have tried ______ browsers, but ______ loads the page correctly. (two / not one)

===
Self-Check Answer Key
1) either (one of two — Wi-Fi or mobile data) 2) Neither (not one, not the other — followed by singular verb "is") 3) Both (the two together — followed by plural verb "passed") 4) both ... neither (tried two browsers; not one of them worked)
Self-check method: check the verb that follows your answer — either/neither always pair with a singular verb, both always pairs with a plural verb, matching the patterns above exactly.

grammar.title: Past Continuous
grammar.explanation: The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at a particular moment in the past, often setting the scene while another event interrupts it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Form it with was (I, he, she, it) or were (you, we, they) + verb-ing: "She was testing the app."; "They were building the drone." Make the negative with not: "They were not paying attention to the screen." Make questions by swapping the subject and was/were: "Were they coding all afternoon?" Two background actions can run at the same time: "While the students were coding, the teacher was checking the server."
grammar.commonMistake: Matching the wrong form of be to the subject ("They was building the drone") or dropping the -ing from the main verb ("She was test the app").
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the past continuous as a video already playing in the background — the action was ongoing, like a live stream you can replay in your mind.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence using the past continuous: 1) Yesterday at 4 PM, I ______ (research) future farming techniques. 2) While she ______ (present) her project, the Wi-Fi disconnected. 3) They ______ (not listen) when the teacher explained the coding task. 4) ______ he ______ (use) the drone when it ran out of battery? 5) The students ______ (converge) in the lab when the alarm sounded.

===
Self-Check Answer Key
1) was researching 2) was presenting 3) were not listening (weren't listening) 4) Was he using 5) were converging
Self-check method: confirm was/were matches the subject (I/he/she/it = was; you/we/they = were) and the main verb keeps its -ing ending, as in the models above "She was testing..." and "They were building...".

grammar.title: Complex Noun Phrases
grammar.explanation: A complex noun phrase builds extra detail around a noun, so instead of "a system" you can write "a solar-powered, automated irrigation system" and give the reader a far more precise picture.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Start with the main noun, then add modifiers around it: adjectives before it ("a fast, reliable connection"), hyphenated compound modifiers ("a solar-powered irrigation system"; "a user-friendly platform"), and prepositional phrases or relative clauses after it ("the sensor in the field"; "the app that monitors soil moisture"). Technology writing often stacks several: "a small, lightweight, waterproof sensor"; "a rudimentary, student-built weather-monitoring application"; "the high-resolution agricultural drone that photographed the fields".
grammar.commonMistake: Piling up modifiers without punctuation, as in "a solar powered automated water delivery device" — coordinate adjectives need commas and compound modifiers need hyphens: "a solar-powered, automated water-delivery device".
grammar.memoryTip: Think of a complex noun phrase as a super noun: the noun is the core and every modifier is an upgrade, like adding features to an app.
grammar.practice:
Part A — build a complex noun phrase from the parts, then use it in a sentence: 1) noun: drone; modifiers: small, solar-powered, lightweight. 2) noun: platform; modifiers: free, open-source, multilingual, coding. 3) noun: sensor; modifiers: the, waterproof, that measures soil moisture.
Part B — expand each simple noun with at least two modifiers: 4) a phone 5) a drone 6) a system 7) an app.
Part C — combine the words in brackets into one phrase and use it in a sentence: 8) (small / portable / solar-powered) + charger 9) (innovative / student-designed / weather-monitoring) + application 10) (high-resolution / lightweight / agricultural) + drone 11) (free / open-source / multilingual) + coding platform.

===
Self-Check Answer Key
Note: Parts A-C ask you to build and use your own noun phrases, so full sentences are open-ended — there is no single correct sentence. However, the phrase itself follows fixed punctuation/hyphenation rules from the rule and examples above that you can check against:
Part A — correctly built phrases: 1) "a small, solar-powered, lightweight drone" (coordinate adjectives "small" and "lightweight" separated by commas; "solar-powered" hyphenated as a compound modifier). Model sentence: "The farmers use a small, solar-powered, lightweight drone to check the fields every morning." 2) "a free, open-source, multilingual coding platform" ("coding" sits closest to the noun as the tightest modifier; "open-source" hyphenated; other adjectives comma-separated). Model sentence: "Students downloaded a free, open-source, multilingual coding platform to build their apps." 3) "the waterproof sensor that measures soil moisture" (article first, adjective next, relative clause after the noun). Model sentence: "The waterproof sensor that measures soil moisture sends an alert when the soil is dry."
Part B — fully open (no fixed modifiers given); model examples only: 4) "a lightweight, waterproof phone" 5) "a small, solar-powered drone" 6) "an automated, easy-to-use irrigation system" 7) "a free, user-friendly coding app".
Part C — correctly built phrases: 8) "a small, portable, solar-powered charger". Model sentence: "She packed a small, portable, solar-powered charger for the camping trip." 9) "an innovative, student-designed, weather-monitoring application". Model sentence: "The team presented an innovative, student-designed, weather-monitoring application at the science fair." 10) "a high-resolution, lightweight, agricultural drone". Model sentence: "The farmer flew a high-resolution, lightweight, agricultural drone over the fields." 11) "a free, open-source, multilingual coding platform". Model sentence: "Volunteers built a free, open-source, multilingual coding platform for schools."
Self-check method: check your phrase against the common-mistake note — coordinate adjectives need commas, compound modifiers need hyphens (e.g. "solar-powered", "student-designed", "weather-monitoring", "high-resolution"). If your phrase is punctuated that way and your sentence uses it as a noun, you are correct — the exact wording of your sentence can differ from the models above.

grammar.title: Adjective + Infinitive, and Verb + -ing
grammar.explanation: An adjective followed by to + base verb expresses feelings and judgements ("easy to use"), while certain verbs and every preposition are followed by the -ing form ("enjoy coding"; "good at building").
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Part 1 — Adjective + infinitive: choose an adjective such as easy, difficult, eager, important, safe or dangerous, then add to + base verb: "It is difficult to omit important data from a report."; "She was eager to acquire the latest coding skills."; "The app is easy to use even for beginners."
Part 2 — Verb + -ing: after enjoy, avoid, consider, keep, suggest and practise, use the -ing form: "They avoided revealing too much information."; "She kept jostling for access to the computer." The -ing form also works as the subject of a sentence ("Coding is a useful skill for the future.") and after prepositions ("He is good at building circuits."). Spelling: drop a final -e (make becomes making) and double a final consonant after a short vowel (sit becomes sitting).
grammar.commonMistake: Using a gerund after an adjective ("It is difficult omitting a key detail") or an infinitive after enjoy or avoid ("I enjoy to code") — the two patterns must not swap places.
grammar.memoryTip: Adjectives love to describe, so they take to + verb; after enjoy, avoid, consider, keep, suggest and practise, say "I enjoy doing", never "I enjoy to do".
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete with the adjective + infinitive: 1) It is ______ (important) ______ (check) your sources before sharing news online. 2) The students were ______ (excited) ______ (present) their app at the science fair. 3) It is ______ (dangerous) ______ (share) personal information on social media. 4) He was ______ (happy) ______ (reveal) the results of his experiment.
Part B — complete with the -ing form: 5) They enjoy ______ (build) robots in their after-school club. 6) She is good at ______ (solve) coding problems quickly. 7) We talked about ______ (create) a school tech blog. 8) He avoided ______ (share) unverified information online. 9) ______ (Learn) to code takes patience and practice.

===
Self-Check Answer Key
Part A (adjective + infinitive): 1) important to check 2) excited to present 3) dangerous to share 4) happy to reveal
Part B (verb + -ing): 5) building 6) solving 7) creating 8) sharing 9) Learning
Self-check method: for Part A, confirm the pattern is adjective + "to" + base verb (never adjective + -ing), matching "easy to use" in the rule and examples above. For Part B, confirm the -ing form follows enjoy/good at/talked about/avoided or starts the sentence as a subject, matching "enjoy coding" and "good at building" — never adjective + infinitive in these slots.

writing.title: Writing 1: Debate Essay — Helping or Harming?
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a structured debate argument of about 250 words for or against this statement: "Technology is doing more harm than good to young people." Open with your position, give three main points with evidence or examples using conditionals ("If young people spend too much time on screens, they will..."), acknowledge the other side with reported speech ("Some people have said that..."), and close with a conclusion that summarises your view.
writing.modelText:
I would like to argue that technology is doing more good than harm to young people.
First, if students use the internet carefully, they will acquire skills that school alone cannot teach: Kofi's coding club built a quiz app in one term. Second, unless we recognise how much learning is now free online, we ignore a huge gift. Third, if young people stay connected with friends and family, they will feel less alone.
Some parents have said that coding is a waste of time and that screens make grades worse. That view is understandable, but adequate limits solve most of the problems.
In conclusion, technology helps young people if it is used with care and purpose.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: Position: I would like to argue that technology is doing more good than harm to young people.

Three points with conditionals: First, if students use the internet carefully, they will acquire skills that school alone cannot teach: our own coding club built a working weather app in a single term. Second, unless we recognise how much learning is now available for free online, from language lessons to science videos, we ignore a genuine gift. Third, if young people stay connected with friends and family who live far away, they will feel less isolated than earlier generations often did.

Acknowledging the other side, reported speech: Some parents have said that screens make homework grades worse and that social media wastes valuable time. That view is understandable, and it is true for students who lose all sense of limits, but reasonable time limits solve most of the problem without banning technology altogether.
Conclusion: In conclusion, technology helps young people far more than it harms them, provided it is used with care, purpose and a sensible limit on screen time.
otherAnswers: A learner arguing the opposite position might open with "I would like to argue that technology is doing more harm than good to young people," and give points such as: if students spend hours scrolling, they will lose time for sleep and homework; unless screen use is limited, attention spans will suffer; if constant comparison online continues, some young people will feel worse about themselves rather than better.

That opposing essay might acknowledge the other side by writing "Some people have said that the internet offers valuable free learning, and that is true, but easy access to distraction cancels out much of that benefit for many students."

writing.title: Writing 2: Digital Detox Diary
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you spend one full week without any digital devices — no phone, no tablet, no computer, no television. Write a diary covering three days of that week, about 250 words in total. For each day, describe what you did instead of using technology, how you felt using precise adjectives and one complex noun phrase, what someone said to you about the experiment reported indirectly ("My mother told me that she was proud of me."), and what you learned about your relationship with technology.
writing.modelText:
Day 1
Without my phone I felt agitated and restless. I helped Mum in the shop and read an old comic. She told me that I looked calmer already, but I was not sure.
Day 3
I played football with Idris until sunset. The long, quiet evening without a single notification felt strange but peaceful. My uncle said that he had grown up like this every day.
Day 6
Today I drew for two hours on the roof. My teacher told me that my sketches were the best she had seen. This week has revealed something: my relationship with technology needs balance, not a lull or a flood.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: Day 1: Without my phone, I felt agitated and oddly bored, the restless kind of boredom I had almost forgotten. I spent the afternoon helping my grandmother sort old photographs instead of scrolling through new ones. She told me that I seemed more present than usual, though I was not entirely sure what she meant by that.

Day 3: I played volleyball with my neighbours until the streetlights came on, something I usually skip because I am busy messaging people I will see the next day anyway. The long, unhurried evening without a single notification felt strange at first but slowly turned peaceful. My father said that he had spent almost every evening of his own childhood exactly like this.

Day 6: Today I taught myself to whittle a small wooden spoon, a slow and frustrating skill that no video could have rushed for me. My aunt told me that my patience had clearly grown over the week. This experiment has revealed something important: my relationship with technology needs balance, not a total absence and not a constant flood.

writing.title: Writing 3: Future Farming Report
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short report of about 250 words describing how technology could improve farming in your region over the next ten years. Explain the current challenges farmers face, present two or three solutions each described with a complex noun phrase (such as drones, smart sensors or solar-powered irrigation), make conditional predictions ("If farmers adopt these technologies, yields will..."; "Unless investment increases, farmers will..."), report the words of an invented expert in indirect speech, and finish with your own opinion on the future of farming.
writing.modelText:
Farmers near our town face a serious problem: rainfall is unpredictable, so crops fail and food prices grow worse each season.
Versatile technology can help. Small solar-powered irrigation pumps along the river could water fields in the dry months. Cheap soil sensors linked to a phone app would reveal exactly when a field needs water.
If farmers acquire these tools, yields will rise. Unless investment in training increases, farmers will lack adequate skills to use them. Dr Amina Warsame, an agricultural scientist, said that the next ten years would determine whether small farms survived.
In my opinion, farming here has a hopeful future if young people and farmers work together.
writing.sentenceStarter: I would like to argue or explain...

items: Challenges: Farmers near our village face a serious problem: unpredictable rainfall makes it impossible to plan planting season with any confidence, so crops fail and food prices rise a little more each year.

Solutions, complex noun phrases: Affordable technology could help. Small solar-powered water pumps installed along the seasonal river could irrigate fields even during the driest months. Cheap soil-moisture sensors connected to an ordinary mobile phone would tell a farmer exactly when a crop actually needs water, instead of guessing.

Conditional predictions and expert quote: If farmers adopt these tools, yields will almost certainly rise within a few seasons. Unless training and financing improve at the same time, however, many farmers will lack the skills or the money to use this equipment properly. Dr Hodan Yusuf, an agricultural researcher, said that the next decade would decide whether small family farms in our region survived at all.
Opinion: In my opinion, farming here has a genuinely hopeful future, but only if young people, farmers and local banks work together instead of waiting for someone else to act first.
otherAnswers: A learner focused on livestock might instead propose mobile veterinary apps and solar-powered cold storage for milk, arguing that if spoilage drops, farmers' incomes will rise even without new irrigation.
A learner focused on markets might propose a simple text-message price-alert system, so that unless farmers know real market prices before travelling, middlemen will keep underpaying them.

To show or make something known that was hidden or secret. The data analysis revealed that the sensor was sending incorrect readings.
reveal — to show or make something known that was hidden or secret. The passage says digital technology has begun to reveal new possibilities for communities across East Africa.
recognise — to see or hear something and know what it is. In part 2, Amal speaks about the need to recognise misinformation and to give people space to explain.
acquire — to get or gain something through effort or learning. The students decided to acquire basic coding skills and build a simple weather-monitoring app.
determine — to find out or decide something after thinking about it. Amal tells Mr. Tariq that it was difficult to determine what to omit from her article.
blunt — speaking in a direct, honest way without trying to be polite. The story introduces Mr. Tariq as a patient, blunt man who runs the school robotics lab.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "The Digital World and Future Innovation" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'agitate'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Smart Farms and Digital Dreams" was about in their own words, and what happened in "Shadows in the Feed, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Present Perfect with Just, and Reported Speech" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
